human_tolerance.notes: Occupies towns and outbuildings readily, sheltering in burrows, holes and even under houses, and is often persecuted by people who mistake it for a large rat.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Judgement. The article describes a breeding season and greater numbers of young in the wetter season but gives no calendar dates; a warm-season window is used for a South American marsupial.

vocalizations.description: A loud, hoarse hiss with the mouth open, used in threat; the animal also barks and squeals when disturbed at night.
A rapid clicking chatter used between individuals at a shared burrow or feeding site.

taxonomy.note: Rank and accepted name from the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy.

external.note: GBIF usage key from the GBIF Backbone match for the scientific name; iNaturalist taxon id and Wikidata Q-id from Wikidata.

conservation.note: The article's taxobox gives the IUCN status as LC.

range.note: 'White-eared opossums ... are commonly found in Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay, Bolivia, Brazil, the Andes, and humid forests of Guyana, Suriname, and southern Venezuela.' The country list is the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 form of that sentence.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: The Spanish article describes 'manos con pulgares oponibles' (opposable thumbs on the hands) and an animal that shelters in burrows, holes and under houses, so the gaits are Walk, Climb and Burrow. Swimming is not described.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: Not sourced. Judgement for a medium-sized didelphid, scaled from the stated head-and-body length of 41-70 cm and the body shape described ('su apariencia general ... recuerda a un cerdo pequeno, un zorro o un gran raton'). This is an estimate, not a sourced figure.

traits.skin.note: 'The white-eared opossum ... has black and grey fur, with white hair covering their ears and face, and dark hair on their long tails.'

traits.nest_type.note: 'some will group together in burrows, holes, empty garbage or even under houses' - the animal shelters and rears young in burrows and holes, which the schema calls a Burrow.

traits.perching.note: The animal walks, climbs and digs; it is not described as perching, and its posture is terrestrial and low to the ground.

traits.mass_kg.note: EltonTraits 1.0 MamFuncDat row for Didelphis albiventris: BodyMass-Value 904 g. The English article's 'about one to three pounds' (roughly 0.45-1.36 kg) and the Spanish article's 500 g to 2 kg bracket the same figure.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 'El peso en los adultos varia entre los 500 grs y los 2 kgs.'

traits.length_m.note: The Spanish article gives head-and-body length by sex: 'los machos suelen medir entre 45 y 70 cm de longitud, mientras que las hembras ... entre 41 y 60 cm'. Midpoint of the whole stated span, 41-70 cm, giving about 0.55 m; the separate 40-65 cm tail is not included, matching how the schema's length_m is used elsewhere in the repository.

traits.lifespan_y.note: No open-licensed source gives a typical or maximum lifespan for Didelphis albiventris: the English and Spanish Wikipedia articles, Wikidata and GBIF carry none, and the field-guide and Animal Diversity Web pages were avoided under the licence policy. 3.0 years is a documented judgement placeholder for a small marsupial, not a sourced figure.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits 1.0 MamFuncDat row for Didelphis albiventris: Diet-Inv 20, Diet-Vunk 30, Diet-Scav 30, Diet-PlantO 20 (Diet-Inv plus Diet-PlantO are carried into the record's invertebrate and fruit shares as the article groups them). The article is explicit: 'They are omnivorous, feeding on invertebrates, small vertebrates, and fruits', and 'South American opossums mainly consume invertebrates such as beetles, diplopods, and opiliones, together with fruit and vertebrates like small birds, mammals, fossorial snakes, and fish.'

traits.social.note: 'Though normally solitary and nomadic, some will group together in burrows, holes, empty garbage or even under houses.' group_size spans a single animal to a pair sharing a burrow.

traits.activity_pattern.note: EltonTraits 1.0 MamFuncDat Activity-Nocturnal 1, Activity-Crepuscular 0, Activity-Diurnal 0 for Didelphis albiventris. The English article's 'begin venturing out for food' for newly weaned young is consistent with night foraging.

traits.defense.note: The Spanish article notes the naked pink nose and long whiskers and that the animal is mistakenly persecuted; the record uses Flee, with the loud open-mouth hiss carried as the alarm call.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement from the described nocturnal behaviour, its fear of people, and its persecution as a supposed pest.

habitat.use.note: 'White-eared opossums inhabit open areas, mountains, and deciduous forests' and shelter in burrows, holes and under houses; the ground-heavy 0.8/0.2 split is a judgement from that, since EltonTraits 1.0 carries no foraging-stratum fields for this species.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'some will group together in burrows, holes, empty garbage or even under houses' - the animal rests and sleeps in burrows and holes.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow the EltonTraits diet shares, with Diet-Vunk carried into the schema's vertebrate share; the burrow shelter weight of 0.9 reflects the described use of burrows and holes, and compost stands for the scavenging the article describes at garbage and under houses.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: urban_affinity and uses_gardens from the described sheltering under houses and in holes in populated areas; light_max is high because the animal is active at night, and road_mortality is judgement.

seasonal.strategy.note: The animal is described as shifting habitat with its breeding season and occurring in warm temperate to subtropical South America year-round, with no migration or hibernation described.

seasonal.phases.note: 'Usually populations are higher in the wetter seasons when the young are weaned and begin venturing out for food' and the animal 'often changes its habitat depending on its breeding season'; the phase dates are a judgement for a warm-season breeding period.

seasonal.life_stages.note: The article describes a marsupial carrying and weaning its young but gives no day counts; duration_days 90 and scale 0.5 are a documented judgement for the pouch and weaning period, not a sourced figure.

vocalizations.alarm.note: The article describes the animal's hissing and vocal defence and records it at night; the description is written from that account.

vocalizations.chatter.note: The article's account of animals gathering in burrows and holes, and foraging in groups when young are weaned, supports a contact call; the description is written from that account and no published description of the call was found.

look.note: 'La cabeza es chata y se extiende hacia adelante con un hocico largo y puntiagudo similar al de un zorro ... con la nariz desnuda de color rosado. La cabeza y las orejas son de color blanco y generalmente tienen una base color negro, además, sobre ella, y extendiéndose verticalmente entre el medio de sus ojos y hasta la nuca, posee una tercera franja de color negro. Sus orejas, redondas y grandes' - the head and ears are white over a black base, with a third black stripe running from between the eyes to the nape, a pink nose, large round ears and a long dark tail. The head is therefore painted the dark body colour and only the ears take the near-white accent, so the model reads as a dark-faced animal with pale ears rather than a white-headed one. Proportions and extra-part placement are judgement.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program: fruit-based nocturnal foraging with a walking gait and a trotting escape, the program's default sun window for a nocturnal species, and flee and calm distances for a wary marsupial.
